verdict.rationale: The original-language data pulls in two directions and supports no single reading. Ephesians 2:11-22 in its original words describes Jew and Gentile fused into 'one new man' (hena kainon anthrōpon) and reconciled in 'one body' (heni sōmati), with the 'dividing wall' (mesotoichon tou phragmou) 'abolished' (katargēsas, a completed past action participle of katargeō, meaning to render inoperative), and Galatians 3:28-29 calls believers 'one' (heis) in Christ and Abraham's 'seed' (sperma), which favors continuity and merger. But Romans 11:25-29 keeps 'all Israel' (pas Israēl) as a future-saved entity distinct from 'the fullness of the Gentiles' (plērōma tōn ethnōn), with the gifts and calling 'irrevocable' (ametamelēta), and Romans 11:17-24 calls Israel the 'natural branches' (kata physin, by nature) of the cultivated 'olive tree' (elaia) into which 'wild olive' (agrielaios) Gentile branches are grafted, which favors an enduring distinction within ONE tree. The naming term 'household management' or 'stewardship' (oikonomia, used at Ephesians 1:10, Ephesians 3:2, Ephesians 3:9, plus 1 Corinthians 9:17, Colossians 1:25, 1 Timothy 1:4, and Luke 16) in all 9 New Testament uses means household management or stewardship, not a sealed-off redemptive epoch, so the lexicon does not by itself license the strong two-programs framing. The verdict turns on framework, not on word meaning, so it is disputed.

scripture.force: 'The fullness of the Gentiles' (plērōma tōn ethnōn) is set alongside a hardening upon Israel that is partial and time-bounded ('in part' apo merous, 'until' achri hou). Israel and the Gentiles function as two named referents within one unfolding sequence, which a distinct-programs reading leans on but a single-program reading reads as one staged plan.

'And so all Israel will be saved' (pas Israēl sōthēsetai) keeps Israel as a standing corporate referent with a future salvation, citing the deliverer from Zion. The persistence of the proper name Israel after the Gentile ingrafting is the original-language hook for an enduring distinction.

'For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable' (ametamelēta gar ta charismata kai hē klēsis tou theou) states that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. The adjective 'irrevocable' (ametamelēta, literally 'not to be repented of') grounds the claim that God's commitments to ethnic Israel are not annulled, which supports a continuing distinct standing for Israel.

Some of the 'branches' (kladōn) were broken off and you, being a 'wild olive' (agrielaios, G0065, a word that occurs only once in the New Testament), were 'grafted in' (enekentristhēs, from engkentrizō G1461) among them and became a fellow partaker of the 'root' (rhiza) and fatness of the 'olive tree' (elaias). The Gentiles enter THE existing olive tree, not a parallel tree. One single 'olive tree' (elaia) with two kinds of branches frames one redemptive plant in the original Greek, not two programs.

If you were cut out of 'an olive tree wild by nature' (kata physin agrielaiou) and grafted 'contrary to nature' (para physin) into a 'cultivated olive' (kallielaion), how much more these 'the natural branches' (hoi kata physin, those by nature) be grafted back into 'their own olive tree' (tēn idian elaian). The phrase 'their own olive' (idian elaian) keeps the natural branches indexed to the same tree and pushes back on a separate-plant framing, while preserving Israel as the natural-branch referent.

The Abrahamic promise makes Abraham 'a great nation' (goy gadol) and a channel of blessing. The Hebrew noun 'nation' (goy) denotes a concrete ethnic and political people, the original-language root of any program directed to a distinct national Israel.

'All the families of the ground' (kol mishpechot ha-adamah) are blessed in Abraham. The universal scope of the blessing, reaching every family, is the original-language basis for reading the Abrahamic promise as one program that ultimately gathers the nations rather than running on a separate track.

'For a stewardship of the fullness of the times' (eis oikonomian tou plērōmatos tōn kairōn), to 'head up all things in Christ' (anakephalaiōsasthai ta panta en tō Christō). The combination of 'household management or stewardship' (oikonomia) plus 'appointed time or season' (kairos) is the strongest text the dispensational name leans on, BUT 'stewardship' (oikonomia) means household management or stewardship and 'to sum up or head up' (anakephalaioomai) names a single converging fulfillment rather than disjunct epochs.

'The stewardship of the grace of God given to me for you' (tēn oikonomian tēs charitos tou theou tēs dotheisēs moi eis hymas). 'Stewardship' (oikonomia) here is Paul's apostolic stewardship of a single grace toward the Gentiles, not a sealed-off era. The from-X grammatical form 'of grace' (tēs charitos) names what is stewarded, the grace itself, one grace, given for both audiences.

'It is not yours to know times or seasons which the Father has set' (ouch hymōn estin gnōnai chronous ē kairous hous ho patēr etheto). The paired 'times' (chronous) and 'seasons' (kairous) names epochs the Father has fixed, which a distinct-programs reading takes as ratifying time-periodization. The text affirms there ARE such times, but does not enumerate them or name an Israel and Church distinction as their content.

'Until times of restoration of all things' (achri chronōn apokatastaseōs pantōn). The word 'restoration' (apokatastasis), which occurs only once in the New Testament, points to a future restoration that the dispensational lens reads as the kingdom restored to Israel (Acts 1:6 'will you restore' apokathistaneis) and the covenantal lens reads as cosmic restoration in Christ. The text supplies the noun but not the referential scope.

'Cutting straight the word of truth' (orthotomounta ton logon tēs alētheias). 'Cutting straight' (orthotomeō) occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense cannot be triangulated from the rest of Scripture. Etymologically it means 'cut straight'; the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, often abbreviated LXX) usage in Proverbs 3:6 and Proverbs 11:5 means 'make a straight path'. The classic dispensational gloss 'rightly dividing' leans on this single occurrence, but the original-language evidence for that sense is one verse only.

Christ made 'the both' (ta amphotera) 'one' (hen) and broke down 'the dividing wall of the fence' (to mesotoichon tou phragmou). The numeral 'one' (hen) applied to the merged Jew and Gentile is the strongest lexical pressure against two permanently distinct programs.

'Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself into one new man' (tēn echthran en tē sarki autou, ton nomon tōn entolōn en dogmasin katargēsas, hina tous dyo ktisē en hautō eis hena kainon anthrōpon). The completed past action participle 'having abolished' (katargēsas, from katargeō, 27 New Testament uses meaning abolish or render inoperative) applied to the law of commandments in decrees, with 'create the two into one new man' (tous dyo ktisē eis hena kainon anthrōpon), names creation ('create' ktizō) of one new humanity that did not previously exist. The compound vocabulary ('new' kainos, 'one' heis, 'man/human' anthrōpos, 'create' ktizō, 'abolish' katargeō) is dense and pressures against two parallel peoples on separate programs.

He reconciles 'both' (tous amphoterous) to God in 'one body' (heni sōmati) through the cross. The singular 'body' (sōma) with the numeral 'one' (heni) again names a unified entity, weighing against the distinct-programs proposition.

There is 'no' (ouk eni) Jew nor Greek, for you are all 'one' (heis) in Christ. The leveling formula with 'one' (heis) erases the Jew and Gentile boundary within Christ, supporting a single-people reading.

If you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's 'seed' (sperma) and 'heirs according to promise' (kat' epangelian klēronomoi). Gentile believers are placed inside the Abrahamic 'seed' (sperma) and inheritance, folding them into the one promise line in the original Greek rather than a separate one.

complicating_texts.resolution: The 'one new man' and the abolished dividing wall describe present access and unified standing for Jew and Gentile in Christ. A distinct-programs reading restricts this unity to the Church age and reads it as not annulling a future national program for Israel in Romans 11, so the merger is real but the original-language data does not by itself settle whether the distinction is permanent.

'Having abolished' (katargēsas, the completed past action participle of katargeō, 27 New Testament uses meaning abolish or render inoperative) applied to the law of commandments, with 'create into one new man' (ktisē eis hena kainon anthrōpon), denotes a creative act producing a single new humanity. A distinct-programs reading takes this as describing the Church specifically, leaving Israel's national program as a separate track to be resumed later. The vocabulary is decisive about what Christ DID, but does not rule on what is reserved for a future age.

'All one in Christ' uses 'one' (heis) of standing and inheritance within Christ, not of the erasure of every created or ethnic category. The same letter and Romans 11 keep the proper name Israel in play, so this text complicates the strong distinction without lexically refuting a residual one.

One 'olive tree' (elaia) with 'natural branches' (kata physin, by nature) broken off and wild branches grafted in is a single-plant image, which presses against a fully separate-tree reading. A distinct-programs reading accommodates this by locating the natural branches' restoration in a future stage (Romans 11:23-24 'will be grafted in again' palin enkentristhēsontai), preserving one tree but with a sequenced two-stage administration.

Whether 'all Israel' (pas Israēl) denotes ethnic national Israel as a distinct future-saved body or the total elect of Jews and Gentiles or the believing remnant of Israel across the age is a referential question the original-language data alone cannot decide. The noun 'Israel' and the adverb 'in this manner' (houtōs) carry multiple readings, and Scripture supplies a second sense of Israel at Galatians 6:16 ('the Israel of God', ton Israēl tou theou) that further unsettles the referent. This anchor is left unresolved and is the pivot of the dispute.

'Stewardship' (oikonomia) plus 'fullness of the times' (plērōma tōn kairōn) supplies the dispensational name and a real notion of fulfilled epoch, BUT 'stewardship' (oikonomia) in all 9 New Testament occurrences means stewardship or household management (Luke 16:2-4, 1 Corinthians 9:17, Ephesians 1:10, Ephesians 3:2, Ephesians 3:9, Colossians 1:25, 1 Timothy 1:4), never lexically a sealed-off period with its own salvation arrangement. 'To sum up or head up' (anakephalaioomai) names convergence, not partition. The term gives the framework its NAME without licensing its full TAXONOMY.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied in the bundle, and the cited verses lie outside published CBGM (the genealogical method behind the ECM, the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) scope. The marked readings in the apparatus at Romans 11:25, Ephesians 2:13, Ephesians 2:15, and Ephesians 1:10 are orthographic (spelling) or word-order variations and do not touch the referents 'Israel' (Israēl), 'Gentiles' (ethnē), 'one' (heis), 'stewardship' (oikonomia), or the 'one body', so they do not move the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Romans 11:25-29 keeps 'all Israel' (pas Israēl) and the 'irrevocable' (ametamelēta) gifts and calling distinct from 'the fullness of the Gentiles' (plērōma tōn ethnōn), the Abrahamic land and 'nation' (goy) promises in Genesis 12 remain unfulfilled to ethnic Israel, Ephesians 1:10 names a 'stewardship' (oikonomia) of the fullness of the 'seasons' (kairoi), Acts 1:7 affirms Father-set 'times or seasons' (chronous ē kairous), Acts 3:21 promises 'restoration of all things' (apokatastasis pantōn), and 2 Timothy 2:15 commands 'cutting straight' (orthotomeō) of the word, so this lens reads Scripture as administering distinguishable programs and as keeping ethnic Israel as a continuing referent with promises not yet fulfilled to the Church.

Ephesians 2:11-22 with 'abolish' (katargeō) of the dividing wall, 'create into one new man' (ktizō eis hena kainon anthrōpon), and reconciliation 'in one body' (en heni sōmati) fuses Jew and Gentile, Galatians 3:28-29 makes all believers one and Abraham's seed and 'heirs according to promise' (kat' epangelian), Romans 11:17-24 uses one 'olive tree' (elaia) with natural and wild branches sharing the same root, Genesis 12:3 blesses all families of the earth, and 'stewardship' (oikonomia) in its 9 New Testament uses means stewardship not epoch, so this lens reads one continuous redemptive program with one people across the testaments.

This lens reads Ephesians 2 unity and Galatians 3 incorporation as real fulfillment in one people while granting that Romans 11 leaves room for a future turning of ethnic Israel ('again grafted in', palin enkentristhēsontai), so it affirms continuity of program while preserving a remaining role for Israel within the one olive tree, without endorsing two parallel tracks.

This lens accepts Ephesians 2 present unity in the body of Christ and a single program of redemption while reading Romans 11:26 and Acts 3:21 as preserving a future fulfillment to ethnic Israel within that program, softening the classical hard Israel and Church distinction while keeping 'stewardship' (oikonomia) and the times-language as marking real administrative stages.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the referential scope of 'Israel' (Israēl) in Romans 11 and on whether the Ephesians 2 and Galatians 3 merger texts are read as total or as age-specific, and on whether 'stewardship' (oikonomia) in Ephesians 1:10 names a stewardship of one converging plan or a sealed-off epoch. These are framework decisions layered onto stable word meanings, which is why the original-language layer cannot adjudicate. Lexically 'stewardship' (oikonomia) means stewardship in 9 of 9 New Testament occurrences, and the olive-tree image in Romans 11 is one tree, which weigh against the sharpest two-programs framing, but Romans 11:26-29 with 'irrevocable' (ametamelēta) and Acts 1:7 with 'times and seasons' (chronous kairous) keep an enduring corporate-Israel referent and time-stage vocabulary on the table.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Scripture speaks of God's dealings with ethnic Israel and with the Church; whether these constitute two distinct programs or one continuous redemptive program across the testaments is the matter under examination.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem embeds the dispensational conclusion by asserting distinct programs and explicitly negating one continuous redemptive program. The phrase 'not one continuous redemptive program' preloads the verdict against covenantal continuity. VERDICT-CHANGED: the verdict was derived on the original stem using the neutral form, weighing both lenses without prejudging.

lay_summary: This statement asks whether the Bible runs two separate plans, one for ethnic Israel and one for the Church, rather than a single connected plan across the Old and New Testaments. The original words do not settle this on their own. In Ephesians 2 the text says Christ made Jew and Gentile into 'one new man' and reconciled both in 'one body', using the verb 'to render inoperative' (katargeō) of the wall of separation. Galatians 3 says all believers are 'one' (heis) in Christ and become Abraham's 'seed' (sperma) and heirs of the promise. The Genesis 12 promise to Abraham makes him a great 'nation' (goy in Hebrew) but also says all the families of the earth will be blessed in him. Romans 11 uses the picture of one 'olive tree' (elaia), with natural branches that are Israel and wild branches that are the Gentiles grafted into the same root, not a separate tree. These passages press toward one joined people. At the same time Romans 11 keeps the name Israel in view, says 'all Israel' (pas Israēl) will be saved, and calls the gifts and calling of God 'irrevocable' (ametamelēta), which keeps a continuing place for ethnic Israel. The very term that gives the view its name, the Greek word 'stewardship' (oikonomia) in Ephesians 1 and 3 often translated 'dispensation', in all nine of its New Testament uses means household management or stewardship, including the steward in Luke 16, never lexically a sealed-off era. Acts 1 mentions 'times and seasons' (chronoi and kairoi) set by the Father and Acts 3 mentions 'restoration' (apokatastasis) of all things, so a stage-and-fulfillment vocabulary really is in the text, but the words do not enumerate the stages or assign Israel and the Church to separate tracks. The key unresolved question is what the word Israel refers to in Romans 11, whether the ethnic nation as a distinct future-saved body or the whole company of the saved, and whether the merger in Ephesians 2 is total or age-specific. Word study alone cannot answer that. Readers who start from a distinct-programs framework find support in Romans 11, in the times-language of Acts 1 and 3, and in the term 'stewardship' (oikonomia), while readers who start from a one-program framework find support in Ephesians 2, Galatians 3, and the single olive tree of Romans 11. Because the same stable word meanings fit more than one defensible arrangement, the original-language pattern is genuinely contested rather than clearly for or against the claim.
